# On Getting Lost

Some of my clearest memories are of being lost. I don't mean the dramatic kind, stranded in a desert or missing a flight. I mean the small, pleasant disorientation of realizing you have walked a few streets past the place you meant to be, and that the city has quietly rearranged itself around you. The street names are unfamiliar. The light is different. A bakery you've never noticed smells of cardamom and burnt sugar, and for a few minutes the world feels larger than the version you had been carrying around.

We have made getting lost very hard to do. Phones tell us where we are with a blue dot that never wavers, and they tell us where to turn before we have finished wondering whether we should. This is useful. I use it constantly. But I have started to suspect that something gets lost in the bargain, and that the thing is not just the inconvenience of wrong turns but a particular way of paying attention to the world.

Consider what navigation used to require. Before satellites, a person moving through unfamiliar territory had to build a mental model of the place from scratch. You noticed that the river bent to the east, that the church spire was visible from two different hills, that the road climbed gently after the second bridge. You kept track of how long you had been walking and in what direction, and you adjusted your sense of where you were as you went. Cognitive scientists sometimes call this path integration, and some animals are astonishingly good at it. Desert ants returning to their nests after a long meandering foraging trip can head back in an almost straight line, having tallied their steps and turns the whole way. They are not reading a map. They are constantly updating an internal sense of where home is relative to where they are.

Humans can do this too, though we tend to be worse at it, partly because we rely on landmarks and partly because we rarely practice. Some researchers have found that people who navigate by memorized routes, turning left at the gas station and right at the school, often develop weaker overall spatial models than those who navigate by orientation, who know roughly where north is at all times. The GPS user, in this light, is a bit like a passenger who has memorized a bus timetable without ever seeing the city. The turns are handled. The geography stays vague.

I don't want to sound like a nostalgist about this. I have no wish to abandon the map in my pocket, and I'm not going to pretend that a paper atlas is inherently more honest than a screen. Maps have always been arguments. They choose what to show and what to leave out, which roads get thick lines and which become dotted ones, which neighborhoods are drawn at the scale of a tourist's wandering and which are reduced to a gray smudge. The old maps of the sea, with their sea monsters and their confident coastlines drawn from hearsay, were no more faithful than ours. They were just more visibly human about their uncertainty. Sometimes a mapmaker would write *here be dragons* at the edge of what he did not know, and that phrase still carries a kind of courage. It admits the limit.

Modern maps rarely admit limits. They render everything with the same crisp authority, and this is a subtle form of persuasion. When a route is drawn as a single bright line, we forget that it is one option among many, chosen by an algorithm optimizing for distance or time or traffic. We forget that the street we are being sent down might be quieter and more beautiful than the one we would have chosen, or that the shortcut through the alley runs past a wall covered in faded murals no one would have seen on the main road. Efficiency is a value, but it is not the only one, and it has a way of crowding out the others without announcing itself.

Getting lost, in the good sense, is a way of relaxing that efficiency. It forces you to look. When you don't know where you are, you start reading signs you would otherwise skim. You notice the shape of the roofs, the kinds of trees, the way people greet each other on the sidewalk. You begin to make guesses and test them. "That hill must be the one I saw from the square, so the river should be on my left." Sometimes you are right, and the small satisfaction of it is out of proportion to its importance. Sometimes you are wrong, and you end up somewhere unexpected, which is often the more memorable outcome.

I think there is something here about attention more generally. Attention is not just a matter of how much of it we have but of what it is directed toward and how it is shaped. Being lost pulls attention outward. Knowing exactly where you are and where you're going tends to pull it inward, toward the destination, toward the next notification, toward the small private anxieties that travel with us everywhere. The Japanese poet Bashō wrote about walking through the countryside with a kind of open receptivity, letting the road set the rhythm of his thoughts. He was not lost in any practical sense; he had a route and a purpose. But he had also cultivated a way of moving through space that let the world into the poem. Being a little lost is one way to make room for that.

Lostness also has a social dimension that I find oddly moving. When you are lost in a city where you don't speak the language well, you have to ask people for help, and that asking creates small connections. A woman with a shopping bag points you toward the metro and tells you, unprompted, about the closure on the line you were about to take. A teenager on a bicycle walks his bike two blocks with you because the street you're looking for is hard to find. A shopkeeper draws a crude map on the back of a receipt, and the map is wrong in one important way, but his kindness is not. These moments are fragile and easy to skip when a screen can answer the question silently. They are also, I think, among the most reliable ways we encounter strangers as people rather than as obstacles or background.

None of this means we should throw our phones into the river. It means we might choose lostness deliberately, the way some people choose to fast or to sleep without an alarm. Leave the map closed for one walk a week. Pick a direction and go, and when you come to a fork, pick the path you have not taken before. Accept that you will sometimes circle back to a place you recognize and feel faintly foolish. The foolishness is part of the point. It keeps you honest about how little you actually know about the place where you live.

There is also a deeper version of getting lost that has nothing to do with streets. Most of us have had the experience of finding ourselves in the middle of a life we did not plan, with the landmarks we relied on gone or unrecognizable. A job ends, a relationship dissolves, a body changes in ways no one warned us about, and suddenly the internal map that once told us where we were no longer fits the terrain. This kind of lostness is not pleasant in the way a wrong turn in a foreign city can be pleasant. It is frightening, and it can last a long time. But it has something in common with the smaller version. You are forced to pay attention to what is actually in front of you, because the stories you were using to navigate have stopped working. You start noticing things. You ask people for directions, sometimes literally and sometimes figuratively, and you discover that others have been lost in similar ways and are willing to say so.

I have come to think that the ability to tolerate being lost, even to enjoy it a little, is a form of maturity. It means being able to sit with not knowing without immediately reaching for the nearest answer. In a culture that treats uncertainty as a problem to be solved as quickly as possible, this is a difficult discipline. Every gap in our knowledge seems to call for a search, a query, a quick confirmation. But some gaps are worth leaving open for a while. Some questions get better when you walk around them.

The ants, I suppose, are not troubled by being lost. They do not experience the nest as a destination to be reached quickly. They simply keep track of where they have been and where home lies, and they trust the accumulated sense they have built. There is a lesson there that is almost too obvious to state: we are constantly building an internal sense of where we are, and that sense can be strengthened or allowed to atrophy depending on how we move through the world. If we let the blue dot do all the work, we may arrive at many places without ever quite knowing where we have been.

So I will keep using my phone, and I will keep being grateful for it when I'm running late in an unfamiliar city. But I will also keep a small habit of wandering. I will take the street that looks interesting even when it adds ten minutes. I will ask the old man on the bench which way the river is, and I will listen to his answer even when it sends me in the wrong direction first. I will let myself be a little lost, not as a failure of planning but as a kind of permission. The world is larger than my map of it, and I would rather remember that than forget it in the name of arriving on time.

The best wrong turns I have taken did not get me anywhere I intended to go. They got me somewhere better: a courtyard I would never have found, a conversation I would never have had, a view over rooftops that made me stop and simply look. Getting lost, it turns out, is one of the few ways left to be surprised by a place you thought you already knew. I think that is worth a few minutes of uncertainty. I think it may be worth quite a lot more than that.
